THE TRADITION OF RESPONSE - PART 1

WHAT THIS CHAPTER COVERS
- Part 1: three myths from ancient cultures that try to answer life's key questions (Prometheus, Gilgamesh, a Native American Cherokee creation myth).
- Part 2: evidence of religious behaviour in ancient societies from (a) rites of passage and initiation, (b) rites of burial and sacrifice, (c) sacred art and artefacts.
- Big idea: from the earliest times, humans in all cultures have been involved in the search for meaning.

KEY TERMS
- Rites of passage: rituals or ceremonies that mark and celebrate important changes (transitions) in a person's life from birth until death.
- Myth: a traditional story or symbolic narrative that tries to explain some natural or social happening.
- Cosmos: the universe seen as a well-ordered system.
- Sacred: something set apart as holy and connected with God.
- Neolithic: the New Stone Age - from the beginning of farming (agriculture) to the use of bronze, about 10,000 to 4,500 BCE.
- Megalithic: to do with prehistoric monuments made of, or containing, large stones.
- Radiocarbon dating: a method that estimates the age of something that was once living by measuring the carbon in a sample and comparing it to an international reference standard.
- Cosmology: a theory about the nature of the universe.
- Chaos: disorder and mystery (the opposite of cosmos).
- Anthropology: the study of human culture and society.

WHAT IS A MYTH?
- A myth is a symbolic story, usually of unknown origin and at least partly traditional. It seems to relate to real events and is linked especially with religious belief.
- The word 'myth' comes from the Greek word mythos, meaning word or story.
- Myths try to answer life's key questions - they explain why things are the way they are.
- Myths came BEFORE philosophy and science, so they are the earliest evidence of humanity's search for meaning.
- Myths do not always stand up to scientific testing, but that was never their purpose. Their value is the insight they give into how people explained things before science or philosophy.
- Later, philosophers (see Chapter 2) questioned the mythical view and used reason and logic instead.
- Myths deal with abstract realities, e.g. the changing seasons, the sun, moon and stars, the origins of life.
- They were passed down orally (by word of mouth) from generation to generation as poetry, songs and legends, because they came before writing.
- Early societies tried to understand the cosmos (the order of the universe as a whole). Ancient myths and cosmologies suggest a religious view of existence.
- Through myth and ritual, early societies tried to bring order (cosmos) to the disorder and mystery (chaos) around them. Bringing cosmos to chaos is part of being human.
- Myths are often religious because they deal with the great questions of life. Every major religion has its own collection of myths.

FOUR TYPES OF MYTH
- 1. Cosmic myths: about origins and order; questions of existence and our place in the world (e.g. creation myths).
- 2. Theistic myths: about gods/goddesses, the creator, the ultimate, and providers of meaning (e.g. the myth of Prometheus).
- 3. Hero myths: about individuals and their journeys of discovery and revelation (e.g. Odysseus and Cuchulainn).
- 4. Place/Object myths: about places or objects of great importance (e.g. King Arthur's sword, Newgrange).

THE MYTH OF THE SACRED PLACE
- Some elements are universal (common to all cultures). Almost all mythologies have the myth of the sacred place.
- Every culture tried to understand the relationship between three levels of the world: the underworld, the earth and the heavens.
- A sacred place was created by symbolically bringing these three levels together.
- Some myths mention a sacred pillar or pole - a 'cosmic pillar' - found in myths around the world.
- The sacred place marked a boundary between what was known and what was different and 'other'.
- It usually had an opening to pass from one level to another, e.g. a doorway, roof opening or passageway.
- Communication with the heavens was symbolised by ladders, pillars, mountains or trees (e.g. Jacob's dream of the ladder to the sky).
- The sacred place was the centre of the world. All the world's major religions have a sacred place in their myths and rituals.
- Humans are natural symbol-makers and storytellers (Chapter 3). Story appeals to imagination, captures attention and speaks to emotions, so it is used as a teaching tool.

MYTH 1: PROMETHEUS (ANCIENT GREECE)
- Tries to explain the origin of fire, and of old age, labour, sickness, insanity, vice (immoral behaviour) and passion.
- First recorded account: Greece, late eighth century BCE. Eighth-century Greeks believed Prometheus was the creator of humanity.
- Zeus: father of heaven, grandson of Mother Earth, most powerful of the gods; he controlled them all.
- Prometheus angered Zeus by being too powerful and clever. Zeus withheld fire from humanity.
- Prometheus is a mediator between the divine and mortals - he steals fire from the gods, allowing human advancement.
- Version adapted from The Greek Myths by Robert Graves.
- The story: Zeus was angry with humanity, took their fire and was about to destroy them; Prometheus pleaded with him.
- Prometheus asked Athene (goddess of wisdom) for a 'backstairs' entry to Olympus (home of the gods). She agreed.
- He lit a torch from the Sun, broke off a piece of glowing charcoal, put it into a giant fennel stalk, put out the torch, slipped away and gave fire to mankind.
- Zeus swore revenge. He ordered Hephaestus (god of fire) to make a clay woman; the four Winds breathed life into her; the goddesses adorned her. She was Pandora, the most beautiful woman ever created.
- Pandora was offered to Epimetheus (Prometheus' brother). He refused, because Prometheus had warned him to accept no gift from Zeus. Zeus became even angrier.
- Punishment: Prometheus was chained naked to a pillar; an eagle tore at his liver all day; every night his liver grew back, so the pain never ended.
- Zeus excused his cruelty by claiming Athene had invited Prometheus to Olympus for a secret love affair.
- Alarmed, Epimetheus quickly married Pandora - made by Zeus to be as foolish, mischievous and idle (lazy) as she was beautiful.
- She opened a jar Prometheus had warned Epimetheus to keep closed. In it were all the Spites that plague mankind: Old Age, Labour, Sickness, Insanity, Vice and Passion. They flew out, stung Epimetheus and Pandora and attacked the human race.
- Hope was also shut in the jar. Hope used deception (lies) to discourage humans from taking their own lives in despair.
- Quote: 'On what wings dare he aspire? What the hand dare seize the fire?' - William Blake.
- Art: Prometheus Bound by Peter Paul Rubens; Prometheus statue at the Rockefeller Centre, New York.
KEY QUESTIONS THE PROMETHEUS MYTH ANSWERS
- Where did fire come from? Prometheus stole it from Olympus for mankind.
- Where did suffering come from? Prometheus was sentenced to suffering by Zeus; Pandora opened the sealed jar and released suffering on the world.
- What is hope? Hope is shown as a dishonest force - this reflects Greek thinking at the time.
- What is the nature of Zeus? A vengeful god, a divine presence to be feared.
- What is the nature of good and evil? Zeus is a force for evil; Prometheus is a force for good, defending humanity.

MYTH 2: GILGAMESH (MESOPOTAMIA)
- An extract from the poem 'Epic of Gilgamesh', adapted from The Hero with a Thousand Faces by Joseph Campbell.
- Known throughout Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq); dated as early as 1200 BCE.
- Can be classed as BOTH an object myth and a hero myth.
- Gilgamesh was a legendary king. After the death of his friend Enkidu he went on a dangerous journey to find the secret of eternal life - a potion for immortality to bring back to his people.
- On the way he passed lions guarding the foothills and scorpion men watching the heaven-supporting mountains; reached a paradise garden of flowers, fruits and precious stones; then the sea that surrounds the world.
- In a cave lived a form of the goddess Ishtar, closely veiled. She closed the gate but let him in after hearing his tale.
- Her advice: stop the quest and be content with the mortal joys of life. 'The life that thou art seeking, thou wilt never find. When the gods created man, they put death upon mankind, and held life in their own hands.' She told him to eat well, enjoy himself day and night, dress well, bathe, care for his child and make his wife happy.
- Gilgamesh insisted on going on. He crossed the waters of death by ferry, warned not to touch the waters.
- He met Utnapishtim, the hero of an ancient flood, who told him the flood story.
- Gilgamesh slept for six days. Utnapishtim's wife baked seven loaves and placed them by his head. The ferryman Ursanapi bathed him and gave him fresh clothes.
- Utnapishtim revealed the secret of a plant giving eternal life: like a brier, with a thorn like a rose that pierces the hand. It grew at the bottom of the cosmic sea.
- Gilgamesh tied stones to his feet, dived to the bottom, plucked the plant (it cut his hand), cut off the stones and rose.
- He named it 'In his age, Man becomes young again' and planned to bring it back to Erech.
- On the way home he bathed in a cool waterhole and slept. A serpent smelled the plant's perfume, took it and ate it - and so gained the power of sloughing (shedding) its skin and renewing its youth.
- Gilgamesh woke, sat down and wept.
- The ending is deeply unsatisfying - the central question (the secret to eternal life) is left unanswered.
- Art: tablet V of the Epic (Sulaymaniyah Museum, Iraq); Assyrian palace relief (713-706 BCE) from Dur-Sharrukin, now in the Louvre, thought to show Gilgamesh as Master of Animals.
KEY QUESTIONS THE GILGAMESH MYTH ANSWERS
- Why do we die? Asked after Enkidu's death; it starts his journey.
- Is there such a thing as eternal life? He searches, ignoring advice not to.
- Why do snakes shed their skin? The serpent ate the plant. Snakes were native to the region, so people may have asked this.
- Why do we fear death? His determination shows his fear. In Tablet X he says: 'I too like him will lie down not to rise again for ever and ever?'

MYTH 3: A NATIVE AMERICAN (CHEROKEE) CREATION MYTH
- From the Cherokee people, one of the largest Native American tribes in North America. Shows how they understood the world and the relationship between people and nature.
- Long ago water covered everything. The earth was a great island floating above the seas, hung by four rawhide (animal skin) ropes representing the four sacred directions, from the crystal sky.
- No people; the animals lived above the rainbow.
- Needing space, they sent Water Beetle under the seas. It brought up mud that spread and became land - flat, soft and wet.
- Grandfather Buzzard flew over to check if it had hardened; the wind from his wings created the valleys and mountains (why Cherokee land has so many mountains).
- Animals came down from the rainbow. It was dark, so they pulled the sun out from behind the rainbow - too bright and hot.
- The shamans (ancient priests) placed the sun higher; a path was made so it travels east to west and all share the light.
- The Creator told plants and animals to stay awake seven days and seven nights. Owls and mountain lions managed it and were given the power to see in the dark.
- Of plants, only cedars, spruces and pines stayed awake; they keep their 'hair' (leaves) in winter; others lose theirs.
- People were created last. Women could have babies every seven days; the Creator feared overcrowding, so women could then have only one child per year.
- Myths are not scientifically true but are still a valuable source of information; they show we still struggle to find meaning - a search we share with our ancestors.
KEY QUESTIONS THE CREATION MYTH ANSWERS
- Where did everything come from? Origin of land, water, sun, rainbows, mountains, rivers, animals and people.
- How does the earth stay in the sky? It is suspended by ropes.
- How does the sun move? Shamans placed it high; a path east to west.
- Why can women have babies only once a year? The Creator feared overcrowding.
- Why do only some trees lose leaves in winter? Cedars, spruces and pines stayed awake.
- Why can some animals see in the dark? They stayed awake seven days and nights.
- First form of life: animals (living above the rainbow); people came last.

EXAM TIP
- Pay close attention to the command word - compare, explain, investigate, etc. Do exactly what is asked.

EVIDENCE OF RELIGIOUS BEHAVIOUR IN ANCIENT SOCIETIES
- Evidence-based research means gathering information from the evidence in front of you (like the school bag pair work).
- Ancient people did not separate the secular world from the sacred world.
- Example: the Celts believed the Tuatha De Danann, the main gods of pre-Christian Ireland, lived beneath them and watched everything they did.
- The split between religious awareness and a secular worldview came much later, in the Enlightenment (Chapter 2).
- Philosopher Charles Taylor: our ancestors lived in an 'enchanted world' and we do not. 'We are "buffered" selves. We have changed.' We have a much firmer sense of the boundary between self and other.
- So we can assume the behaviour patterns of ancient societies were religious.

RITES OF PASSAGE AND INITIATION
- Anthropology and archaeology in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries helped us understand ritual in ancient societies. Rites of passage were first identified at the start of the twentieth century.
- Life has transitions: birth, puberty, leaving home, marriage (for early humans, choosing a mate or partner) and death.
- In ancient societies these were marked by special rituals called rites of passage or initiation. They show a need to mark a change in status in a significant way.
- They helped a change happen in the individual and/or community and placed it in the bigger life cycle of birth-death-rebirth.
- They show the early human need to understand and be in harmony with the cosmos - so can be seen as early religious belief.
- They have a similar structure to religious rituals today, helping people cope with questions like: Why am I here? Where am I going? What is my purpose?
- It is hard to prove they were religious, but there are similarities with religious rituals today.
THREE-PART PATTERN
- 1. Separation: the person is separated from peers/family/tribe, or the tribe leaves the place of everyday living.
- 2. Transition: a ritual is enacted, perhaps led by a special person (a parent, a wise person).
- 3. Incorporation: the person rejoins the group with a new way of seeing or living.
- Arnold van Gennep coined the term 'rites of passage' in the early 1900s, in his book The Rites of Passage. His three stages: rites of separation, rites of the margin, rites of incorporation.
- Victor Turner later called the middle stage 'betwixt and between' - no longer in the old role, not yet in the new one.
- Like crossing the threshold of a doorway into a new place.
- Picture example: Maasai young men in Tanzania at a ceremony of transition into a new age group.

CASE STUDY: ABORIGINAL AUSTRALIAN INITIATION (CIRCUMCISION)
- The passage from childhood to adulthood is one of the most important rites in primitive societies.
- Circumcision is a main feature of initiation for Aboriginal Australians. Described by Joseph Campbell in The Hero with a Thousand Faces.
- Murngin tribe (northern Australia):
- The father tells the boy the 'Great Father Snake' is calling him to be circumcised. The boy believes it and is very frightened.
- He hides with his mother or a female relative. The women wail ceremonially to stop the snake swallowing him.
- A horn called Yurlunggur is blown - the call of Great Father Snake.
- When the men come, the women pretend to fight with spears and wail, because he will no longer be their little boy.
- At a dancing ground, over many nights, he is shown dances symbolising his ancestors and taught myths explaining the world.
- He is sent on a long journey to neighbouring clans - symbolic separation from his mother.
- Finally, circumcision. He is now a man in the eyes of the tribe.
- Arunta tribe (central Australia):
- Before the ceremony bullroarers (a musical instrument) sound - they symbolise the voices of the deities.
- A man approaches through firelight balancing a shield on his head; he kneels before the boy.
- The boy's uncles lift him onto the shield while the men chant. The operation is performed; the bullroarers leave; the boy is congratulated by all the men.
- Campbell: the boys are symbolically killed, break past their fear and are reborn into adulthood - moving from dependency to mature authority.

RITES OF BURIAL
- Burial rituals show how ancient societies viewed life, death and the afterlife.
- Formal burial was an important step in the history of ritual - bodies were no longer abandoned or left to wild animals.
- Humans moved beyond accepting death as the end and looked for ways for life to continue beyond death.
- Evidence: ritual burial and/or cremation, special clothing, ornaments on the body, special places and structures.
- Example 1 - Moravia: Karl Maska, an eminent Stone Age archaeologist, in 1984 (date as given in the textbook) found a mass grave 25,000-30,000 years old with eighteen people - ten children and eight adults - buried with ornaments and objects in a large oval pit covered with stone slabs and mammoth bones. No one knows if they were related or why the mammoth bones; something significant was clearly intended.
- Example 2 - Catalhoyuk, south-central Turkey: a Neolithic settlement dated about 6250-5400 BCE. People buried their dead beneath the floors of their houses; each family kept its own burial site and opened it when someone died. This may show a belief that the dead were still part of the living.
- Death was probably surrounded by fear and wonder - one of the great mysteries of life.

RITES OF SACRIFICE
- Sacrifice: giving something of value to a god or gods to show devotion or commitment.
- Ancient Israelites sacrificed animals by ritual burning. Fire symbolised union between those offering and God - YHWH (Yahweh), the God of Abraham and Moses.
- Functions: to please the gods (e.g. for fertile soil for next year's crops); to give thanks for the first fruits of the harvest, believing all life was a gift of the gods.
- Animal sacrifice continued in Jewish worship in the centuries before Christianity.
- Human sacrifice: especially at the burial of a king or great leader - attendants or soldiers killed and buried with him, perhaps to serve him in the afterlife.
- Example 1 - Sumerian royal tombs, Mesopotamia: uncovered in the 1920s-30s by Sir Leonard Woolley; dated (by the textbook) back to 5500 BCE. One tomb: 68 female and 6 male attendants, richly adorned. Another: soldiers, with an ox cart and oxen guarding the entrance. (Picture: Sumerian headdress.)
- Example 2 - Tollund Man: found in 1960 in Tollund Fen (bog), Denmark. Radiocarbon dating: died around 405-380 BCE. The peat bog preserved the body.
- Naked except for a cap and a belt; lying as if asleep with legs drawn up; a noose of plaited animal hide tight around his neck - he had been hanged.
- Hair cropped very short; stubble on chin and lip (had not shaved that day); about forty years old.
- Last meal: porridge with barley, flax, wild weed seeds and some fish.
- Hundreds of bog people have been found; most died violently (hanging, blows to the head, stabbing). Perhaps criminals - but a strong suggestion of ritual sacrifice, supported by vessels, ornaments and artefacts at the sites and the careful way he was buried.
- Conclusion: burial and sacrifice show a sense of the importance of ritual and possibly awareness of a spiritual or religious dimension to life.

SACRED ART AND ARTEFACTS
- Sacred art and artefacts give evidence of religious awareness. Historians and archaeologists are like detectives looking for clues.
- Example: Newgrange, County Meath - Neolithic, around 3200 BCE.
- Evidence of our ancestors' extraordinary skill and of a spiritual dimension to their lives.
- Monuments are astronomically aligned with the movement of the sun - an astonishing feat of engineering even today.
- The mound was used for burial and for rituals connected with the winter solstice.
- Solstice: a moment in the year when the sun is at its furthest north or south of the equator.
- The stones are covered in carved symbols - Megalithic art - spirals and wavy lines, especially on the huge entrance stone.
- Spirals appear at similar sites in many countries, so may have been universal symbols. Some scholars: spirals symbolise the cycle of life and celebrate nature. Others: they symbolise the sun, moon and stars.
- On 21 December (the shortest day) the rising sun shines through the shaft (roof box) above the entrance and lights up the inner chamber.
- After that date days lengthen - for the people, the sun had returned and darkness was defeated. This may have given hope at a dark time of year.
- The builders wanted to be in harmony with the universe and to express a sense of something 'other', even sacred, at the centre of existence.
- Other burial symbols: seeds in a tomb may suggest belief in rebirth or resurrection; red ochre (a red clay) at Neolithic burials may suggest the life-giving power of blood; rich ornaments may show belief in an afterlife or the person's status.
- Conclusion: these rituals and symbols show ancient humans searched for meaning in the face of death and loss.

They were proven true by science
They came before philosophy and science

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what a myth is and why myths were important to ancient people.
rows.model_answer: A myth is a traditional, symbolic story that tries to explain some natural or social happening. Myths came before science and philosophy, so they were the way ancient people explained why things were the way they were, such as the seasons, the sun and stars, and the origins of life. They are the earliest evidence of the human search for meaning.

rows.prompt: Name the four types of myth and give an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Cosmic myths deal with origins and order, e.g. creation myths. Theistic myths deal with gods and goddesses, e.g. the myth of Prometheus. Hero myths deal with individuals and their journeys, e.g. Odysseus and Cuchulainn. Place/Object myths deal with important places or objects, e.g. King Arthur's sword or Newgrange.

rows.prompt: Name three questions about life that the myth of Prometheus tries to answer.
rows.model_answer: It tries to explain where fire came from (Prometheus stole it from Olympus), where suffering came from (Pandora opened the jar and released the Spites such as Old Age and Sickness), and what the nature of Zeus is (a vengeful god to be feared). It also explores what hope is and the nature of good and evil.

rows.prompt: Explain why the ending of the Gilgamesh myth is described as 'deeply unsatisfying'.
rows.model_answer: Gilgamesh goes through great danger and finally finds the plant that would give eternal life, but while he sleeps a serpent eats it. He wakes and weeps. The question at the centre of the myth, the secret to eternal life, is left unanswered.

rows.prompt: Name two natural features the Cherokee creation myth explains and say how it explains them.
rows.model_answer: It explains why some trees keep their leaves in winter: cedars, spruces and pines stayed awake for seven days and nights and were allowed to keep their 'hair'. It explains how the sun moves: the shamans placed it higher in the sky and made a path for it from east to west so all could share the light.

rows.prompt: Outline the three elements found in rites of passage.
rows.model_answer: First is separation, where the person is separated from family, peers or tribe. Second is transition, where a ritual is carried out, often led by a special person such as a parent or wise person. Third is incorporation, where the person rejoins the group with a new way of seeing or living. Van Gennep called these rites of separation, of the margin, and of incorporation.

rows.prompt: Explain what a rite of sacrifice is and give two reasons ancient people offered sacrifice.
rows.model_answer: A rite of sacrifice is giving something of value to a god or gods to show devotion or commitment. Ancient people offered sacrifice to please the gods, for example to make the soil fertile for next year's crops. They also offered it in thanksgiving for the first fruits of the harvest, believing that all life was a gift from the gods.

rows.prompt: What evidence of religious belief can be seen at Newgrange?
rows.model_answer: Newgrange (about 3200 BCE) was used for burial and for rituals linked to the winter solstice. It is aligned so that on 21 December the rising sun lights up the inner chamber, which may have symbolised the defeat of darkness and given hope. Its spirals and wavy lines (Megalithic art) may symbolise the cycle of life or the sun, moon and stars, showing a sense of something sacred at the centre of existence.

rows.prompt: Compare the way in which questions about the meaning of life are addressed in two myths from ancient times that you have studied.
rows.model_answer:
The myth of Prometheus from ancient Greece (first recorded in the late eighth century BCE) and the Epic of Gilgamesh from Mesopotamia (dated as early as 1200 BCE) both deal with suffering and death. In the Prometheus myth, Prometheus steals fire from Olympus, hiding a piece of charcoal in a fennel stalk, to help humanity. Zeus takes revenge by chaining him to a pillar where an eagle eats his liver every day, and by sending Pandora, who opens a jar releasing Old Age, Labour, Sickness, Insanity, Vice and Passion. The myth answers where fire and suffering come from, and shows Zeus as a vengeful god to be feared and hope as a dishonest force.

The Gilgamesh myth asks 'Why do we die?' after the death of Enkidu. Gilgamesh travels past lions and scorpion men, ignores Ishtar's advice to enjoy mortal life, and dives to the bottom of the cosmic sea for a plant of eternal life, which a serpent then eats. It also explains why snakes shed their skin.

Similarity: both try to explain why humans suffer and die, and both show the gods holding power over humans. Difference: Prometheus gives an answer (suffering came from Pandora's jar), while Gilgamesh leaves the question of eternal life unanswered, ending with the hero weeping.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Must name and describe two myths and make real comparison (similarities and differences). May refer to: Prometheus stealing fire; Pandora's jar and the Spites; hope as dishonest; Zeus as vengeful; Gilgamesh and Enkidu; Ishtar's advice; plant of eternal life; serpent shedding its skin; both explain suffering/death; one answers, one leaves question open.

rows.prompt: Describe one rite of passage from an ancient society and explain how it shows the human search for meaning.
rows.model_answer:
One rite of passage is the initiation of boys into manhood among the Murngin tribe of northern Australia, described by Joseph Campbell in The Hero with a Thousand Faces. The father tells the boy that the 'Great Father Snake' is calling him to be circumcised. The frightened boy hides with his mother, and the women wail to stop the snake swallowing him. A horn called Yurlunggur is blown, symbolising the snake's call. The women pretend to fight the men with spears. Over many nights at a dancing ground the boy is shown dances symbolising his ancestors and taught myths that explain the world. He is sent on a long journey to neighbouring clans, symbolically separating him from his mother. Finally he is circumcised and is now a man.

This follows the three-part pattern of separation, transition and incorporation identified by Arnold van Gennep. Campbell says the boy is symbolically killed and reborn into adulthood. The rite shows the search for meaning because it places a frightening change within the bigger cycle of birth-death-rebirth, teaches the boy the myths that explain his world, and helps him and the tribe live in harmony with the cosmos.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Description of rite (up to 12) + explanation of link to search for meaning (up to 8). May refer to: Great Father Snake; Yurlunggur horn; women wailing/fighting; dancing ground and ancestor dances; myths taught; journey to clans; circumcision; separation-transition-incorporation; van Gennep; symbolic death and rebirth; birth-death-rebirth cycle; harmony with cosmos.

rows.prompt: Examine how ancient rites of burial AND ancient rites of sacrifice expressed the religious beliefs of people in ancient times.
rows.model_answer:
Rites of burial show that ancient people did not see death simply as the end. Formal burial meant bodies were no longer left to wild animals. In Moravia, Karl Maska found a mass grave 25,000-30,000 years old with ten children and eight adults, buried with ornaments in an oval pit covered with stone slabs and mammoth bones - clearly something significant was intended. At Catalhoyuk in Turkey (about 6250-5400 BCE) people buried their dead beneath their house floors, which may show a belief that the dead were still part of the living. Ornaments, seeds and red ochre in graves may point to belief in an afterlife or rebirth.

Rites of sacrifice involved giving something of value to the gods to show devotion, to please them for good crops, or to give thanks for the first fruits. The Israelites burned animals, the fire symbolising union with Yahweh. Sir Leonard Woolley found Sumerian royal tombs with sixty-eight female and six male attendants, suggesting a belief that servants would serve the ruler in the afterlife. The Tollund Man, found in Denmark in 1960 and dated by radiocarbon to 405-380 BCE, was hanged and carefully buried, strongly suggesting ritual sacrifice. Both kinds of rite show awareness of a spiritual dimension to life.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Both rites must be dealt with (roughly 10 marks each). May refer to: Maska/Moravia grave; Catalhoyuk under-floor burial; ornaments, seeds, red ochre; belief in afterlife; meaning of sacrifice; Israelite burnt offering and Yahweh; fertility and first fruits; Woolley's Sumerian tombs and attendants; Tollund Man, noose, radiocarbon date, careful burial; spiritual dimension.

rows.prompt: Investigate how evidence of religious belief can be seen in one work of art or artefact from ancient times.
rows.model_answer:
Newgrange in County Meath dates from the Neolithic period, around 3200 BCE. It shows both the great skill of our ancestors and a spiritual dimension to their lives. The mound was used for burial and for rituals linked to the winter solstice. It is astronomically aligned so that on 21 December, the shortest day, the rays of the rising sun pass through the shaft above the entrance and fill the inner chamber with light. From then on the days lengthen, so for the people the sun had returned and darkness was defeated. This may have given them hope at the darkest time of year and shows they wanted to live in harmony with the universe.

The stones, especially the huge entrance stone, are carved with Megalithic art: spirals and wavy lines. Because spirals appear at similar sites in many countries they may be universal symbols. Some scholars think they symbolise the cycle of life, others the sun, moon and stars. Together this shows the builders' sense of something 'other', even sacred, at the centre of existence.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: Neolithic, c. 3200 BCE; burial and solstice rituals; alignment with sun; 21 December light in chamber; defeat of darkness and hope; Megalithic art - spirals and wavy lines; entrance stone; meanings of spirals; sense of the sacred/'other'.
